doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Early jazz records, radio and a turn to classical composers
summary: His singer mother, an uncle violinist, and 78s of Bix and Billie Holiday gave him his first jazz; he heard Tatum and Wilson on radio remotes, then grew fond of Bartok, Stravinsky and Hindemith.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What drew you to jazz as a young man?

Well my mother was a part time night club singer. She usually worked days and sang somewhere in San Diego at least a few nights a week. She always loved singing and she was a good singer. And because of that, and also there were some other, I didn’t come from a musician family in the professional sense, but an uncle was a violinist, and we were certainly a music oriented family, and there were some wonderful 78s that I always remember from my earliest childhood memories, that we had in the home, of course before LPs even. Bix Beiderbecke we had, and Billie Holiday specifically. I think maybe also some Eddie Condon and some other great stuff. But I specifically remember the Bix Beiderbecke and Billie Holiday 78s. And my earliest memories of jazz are those records, which is not a bad introduction, and you have to remember too how much more jazz there was, live jazz there was, on the radio in those days. There again that’s virtually nonexistent today. We have one local jazz station at the community college here in San Diego that does have live broadcasts, I think once a month, but in most parts of the country that’s a thing of the past. But there was a lot of live music on the radio in those days. Big bands and smaller groups from the Royal Roost in New York and all kinds of stuff that was on there, they called them remotes, and so you could hear Charlie Parker on the radio. And I don’t remember hearing Bird, I was still too young to have heard those broadcasts or to have been aware of what was going on, but I remember vividly hearing

Art Tatum on the radio, and Teddy Wilson, and those, along with some of the early records that I mentioned that we had in the home I think were what — I was still too young to be thinking in terms of doing it, but at least it made that connection. The sound of that music seemed very special. It seemed very important compared to the pop music of the day. But actually I became more interested in classical music as I got older, and I was really primarily interested in trying writing—
Composing after some of the people that I really admired at that time, they were still relatively modern composers.
Well you know they’re pretty traditional today in a lot of people’s—
